theme: Rail and ground travel: Amtrak ridership, SNCF/DB/Trenitalia open data, Eurostar, bus (FlixBus), rideshare datasets (Uber Movement), NYC TLC airport trips, Chicago taxi

candidates.name: nyc-taxi-data
candidates.what_it_holds: Scripts (R + shell) to download and load 3+ billion NYC taxi and for-hire-vehicle (Uber, Lyft) trip records since 2009 into PostgreSQL or ClickHouse, sourced from official NYC TLC trip-record parquet files (CSV pre-May 2022). TLC records carry pickup/dropoff LocationID fields that include JFK and LaGuardia airport zones, so airport-trip volumes can be isolated. Data not committed to the repo itself (70GB+); pulled via download_raw_data.sh.
candidates.why_useful: Directly addresses gap #10 (rail/road/airport ground-travel capacity and traffic) via airport-connection taxi/rideshare volume as a proxy for air-travel demand into NYC, and general rideshare volume as a consumer-travel-strength read.
candidates.size_hint: 3B+ trip rows (external); repo itself is code only
candidates.license: MIT (code); data is public NYC TLC records

candidates.name: chicago-taxi-data
candidates.what_it_holds: Scripts to download and analyze City of Chicago taxi trip records (~200M rows as of Q1 2020) and Transportation Network Provider/TNP data (Uber/Lyft, ~130M rows), plus census-tract/community-area mapping, weather data, and shapefiles. Data pulled from Chicago's open-data portal (70GB+ CSV), not committed.
candidates.why_useful: Second major US metro ground-travel/rideshare volume series for gap #10; Chicago is a top-10 US market with international airport connections (O'Hare), useful as a cross-check on the NYC TLC series for broader US travel-demand read-through.
candidates.license: Public Chicago open-data portal data; repo code unspecified/MIT-like

candidates.name: uber-tlc-foil-response
candidates.what_it_holds: Committed CSVs from a NYC TLC FOIL response: 4.5M Uber pickups (Apr-Sep 2014, 6 monthly files with lat/lon/base code), 14.3M Uber pickups (Jan-Jun 2015, adds dispatch base + location ID), plus per-company files and an aggregated daily dataset for 329 other for-hire-vehicle companies (Jan-Aug 2015), taxi-zone lookup table, and TLC correspondence PDFs.
candidates.why_useful: Point-in-time historical rideshare-volume snapshot for NYC predating most modern coverage; static and fully committed so it is trivially reproducible without a live pull, useful as an older baseline/backtest period for a ground-travel demand proxy (gap #10).
candidates.size_hint: ~19M Uber pickup rows + company-level FHV aggregates

candidates.name: amtrak-data
candidates.what_it_holds: Amtrak's monthly performance reports extracted (via Tabula from the published PDFs) into JSON/CSV/XML, organized by year and month, covering five tables per month: Operating Results, Capital Results, Key Performance Indicators, Sources and Uses of Cash, and Route-Level Results. Coverage August 2021 to present (maintainer flags update currency as uncertain); raw PDFs and unprocessed tabula extracts kept under /reports.
candidates.why_useful: Directly fills gap #10 (Amtrak/rail traffic) with route-level Amtrak operating and ridership-adjacent metrics at monthly frequency since mid-2021 — the most granular free Amtrak dataset found; useful as a US intercity-rail demand cross-check against ABNB's domestic leisure-travel exposure.
candidates.license: not stated in fetch; derived from Amtrak public PDF reports

candidates.name: deutsche-bahn-data
candidates.what_it_holds: Historical Deutsche Bahn train schedule, delay (minutes late), cancellation (arrival/departure separately), and station data. Raw API responses (parquet-wrapped XML/JSON) and monthly processed parquet files (20 columns: station, train ID, planned/actual times, delay, cancellation flag) for ~100 largest stations Jul 2024-Nov 2025, then all German stations Nov 2025-present (with a known 2025-11 to 2026-07 API-outage gap). Repo git history was rewritten to drop large files; full data now published on Hugging Face. CC BY 4.0 (DB) data licence.
candidates.why_useful: German/European rail punctuality and cancellation-rate time series at near-daily granularity — a EU ground-travel supply/demand and disruption proxy (gap #10) and a possible cancellation-rate methodology analogue for the RNPL/cancellation thesis (gap #3), even though the underlying business (rail) differs from STR bookings.
candidates.size_hint: Monthly parquet files, ~100-all stations x daily train movements
candidates.last_activity: active as of the 2026 README reference

candidates.name: mobility-database-catalogs
candidates.what_it_holds: A global catalog (JSON files per feed + a consolidated CSV at files.mobilitydatabase.org/feeds_v2.csv, plus a Python API) of public GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime feeds worldwide, filterable by country/subdivision/bounding box/status. Not rail-company-specific but a discovery layer for whichever rail/bus GTFS feeds (SNCF TER/Intercités, Trenitalia, FlixBus, regional EU operators) are publicly published.
candidates.why_useful: Matches gap #17 (Socrata/CKAN-style open-data discovery client) applied to transit: a single machine-readable index to find and pull SNCF/DB/Trenitalia/FlixBus schedule (capacity/frequency) feeds without hand-hunting each operator's portal.
candidates.time_coverage: live/current feeds only (schedules, not historical ridership)
candidates.license: repo MIT/Apache-style; underlying feeds vary by operator

candidates.name: eurostar2gtfs
candidates.what_it_holds: TypeScript tool that converts the published Eurostar timetable into a standard GTFS feed (routes, trips, stop times, calendar).
candidates.why_useful: Gives a machine-readable Eurostar schedule/frequency/capacity series (cross-Channel rail capacity) as a minor complement to gap #10's rail coverage; schedule-only, not ridership, so lower standalone value.
candidates.time_coverage: current timetable only, no history committed

candidates.name: transport-site
candidates.what_it_holds: Elixir/Phoenix codebase for transport.data.gouv.fr, France's National Access Point for mobility data — aggregates GTFS/GTFS-RT feeds from ~356 French transit authorities (76.3% population coverage per the site) including regional and national rail/bus operators, with feed validation and proxying tools. The site itself (not this code repo) is the actual place to pull French SNCF-adjacent GTFS feeds.
candidates.why_useful: Points to a comprehensive French national transit-data catalog (potentially including SNCF TER/Intercités GTFS and FlixBus France feeds) that a scraper/analyst could query for schedule/capacity data; the GitHub repo itself is only the platform's code, not the data.

candidates.name: nyc-tlc-hvfhv-data-pipeline
candidates.what_it_holds: Python/DuckDB/GeoPandas/Streamlit pipeline built specifically on NYC TLC's High-Volume For-Hire-Vehicle (Uber/Lyft/Via/Juno) trip-record dataset, described as analyzing 'millions of rideshare trips'.
candidates.why_useful: A second, independent pipeline confirming the official TLC HVFHV rideshare dataset (distinct table from yellow/green taxi) is easily machine-pullable; useful if the team wants ride-hail-specific volumes (as opposed to taxi) split out for airport/ground-travel demand reads.
candidates.time_coverage: not specified in listing; TLC HVFHV data runs 2019-present
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: overlaps with toddwschneider/nyc-taxi-data's FHV coverage, but isolates the HVFHV table specifically

candidates.name: db-rest
candidates.what_it_holds: A live REST API wrapper (now built on db-vendo-client after DB's HAFAS API was retired) exposing Deutsche Bahn station search, timetable, and journey-planning data at v6.db.transport.rest.
candidates.why_useful: A lightweight live-query method for current DB schedules/stations if a point-in-time snapshot approach (repeated pulls) were wanted; no historical store of its own, so lower value than piebro/deutsche-bahn-data for backtesting.

candidates.name: amtrak (amtrak.js / amtraker)
candidates.what_it_holds: NPM/JS client for the community api.amtraker.com API: live Amtrak train GPS positions, speed/heading, station metadata, and planned vs. actual arrival/departure (real-time only, no history stored in the repo).
candidates.why_useful: Could support a rolling on-time-performance / delay-frequency scrape as a service-quality or disruption proxy for Amtrak, complementing piemadd/amtrak-data's monthly financial tables with finer-grained (per-train) timing data, but requires building the historical archive yourself.
candidates.license: Open Data Commons Attribution License (data); repo code licence separate

candidates.name: nyc-citibike-data
candidates.what_it_holds: Scripts to download and analyze NYC Citi Bike system trip data (bike-share) and load into PostgreSQL, from Citi Bike's own public trip-history exports.
candidates.why_useful: Tangential ground-mobility/local-tourism-activity proxy (bike-share usage correlates with short-trip/tourist foot traffic in NYC); marginal fit to the rail/rideshare theme but a real, maintained dataset method worth noting for completeness.
candidates.size_hint: tens of millions of trip rows (external)
candidates.last_activity: companion repo to nyc-taxi-data, periodically maintained

notes: The WebSearch tool's session-wide budget (200/200) was already exhausted by other scouts before this session ran its first query, so all four seed WebSearch queries failed immediately with no results. Bing and DuckDuckGo HTML search via WebFetch were also unusable (Bing ignores site: filtering and returns generic official-site results; DDG HTML returns 403). GitHub's own /search endpoint via WebFetch returned HTTP 429 (rate-limited) after a couple of calls and stayed limited for the rest of the session. Kaggle and Hugging Face's JS-rendered search pages returned no content via WebFetch. The workaround that did work well: GitHub's static /topics/<tag> pages, which are server-rendered and listed real repos directly, plus direct WebFetch verification of specific repo URLs recalled from training knowledge. Dead ends worth flagging to other scouts: Amtrak, SNCF, Trenitalia, FlixBus, Renfe official GitHub orgs are all empty or irrelevant (no ridership data published there); DB's official org (deutschebahn) has no open-data repos either — DB's real open-data activity lives under community/derived repos (piebro/deutsche-bahn-data) and the dbinfrago sub-org (station/API docs, no historical ridership). Uber Movement itself appears to have been fully taken down with no GitHub mirror found (the official movement-data site was discontinued; no archive repo located, topic page uber-movement returns only 2 unrelated repos) — worth a dedicated deeper pass by another scout with fresh WebSearch budget, ideally checking Zenodo/Archive.org directly rather than GitHub. Given the search-tool outages, this scout is likely undercounting genuine repos versus a normal run; a re-run once WebSearch budget resets would probably surface more (e.g., dedicated academic replication packages using Uber Movement CSVs, or European national statistics office rail-ridership GitHub mirrors) that pure GitHub-topics browsing could not reach.
